## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Patrol officers and deputies who write incident reports from body-cam footage.
   [LYC] "Intros to Police, Sheriff, Transit, or University PDs that wrestle with video or paperwork overload."
   [LYC] "We auto-generate reports, verify narratives, and surface evidence instantly — cutting desk time by 60% and
   putting officers where communities need them most." → `roles[officer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.
   Author's choice: "at small and mid-sized police departments" stands for [LYC]'s "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers)".

2. **What (the job).** Get every call written up as a report, accurately, without the officer stuck at the desk.
   [LYC] "40% of a typical shift vanishes to transcribing body-cam footage, filling forms, and locating clips across
   siloed systems." [YCW] "Officers spend up to a third of their shifts manually transcribing body camera footage".
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** After a call, when the footage has to become a report; at the desk, often past end of shift.
   [PR] (Chief Sever) "an officer might not be as detailed if they're 'down 10 reports'". [PR] "End-of-shift reports,
   which provide an overview of incidents over an entire shift, will continue to be written exclusively by humans."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: incident report`. Author's choice: the window {7, DAYS} (spec 120: "every shift"
   reads as 7 DAYS) and Frequency 3 to 5 days out of 7 (an officer works about four or five shifts in seven; the posts
   say "a typical shift", so every shift worked). Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "a typical shift".

4. **Which people.** US police, sheriff, transit and university departments of 10 to 200 officers.
   [LYC] "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers) willing to co-shape features." [LYC] "We'll fly anywhere in North
   America to set you up within 48 hours—no strings attached." → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The department, per officer a month; the chief decides under a spending cap, the city council above it.
   [PR] "Sever said he's only able to authorize expenditures up to a certain amount without Heber City Council approval.
   Purchasing Draft One for around $30,000 per year would require such permission. Buying Code Four at around $6,000 to
   $8,000 per year would not." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: chief}`; Buyer and payer tests "Nobody else" (the
   chief alone), with "The city council" and "The city manager" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A side-by-side
   trial against Axon's tool", is from [PR] ("The Police Department recently completed free trial periods of two AI
   programs") and [CMP] ("We ran 30 days with Axon Draft One and 30 days with Code Four... 17/18 Officers chose Code Four
   at the end of the trial."); the other two items (a records-system check; the prosecutor's office agreeing) are the
   author's, the second from [BDN] (the district attorney: "It's not something that my office, or our PDs, have agreed
   is ready for use."). Commitment's step, "run a free pilot with a few officers": [LYC] "no strings attached"; [BDN]
   "he has provided a year of the software for free"; [PR] the free trial periods. Header: the outside payer (gap 2).

6. **Mechanism.** Footage in; a draft narrative in the department's format, each fact tied to its clip, with check
   words the officer must remove.
   [LYC] "Autofilled narrative reports that match your RMS schema and chain-of-custody rules." [LYC] "Real-time
   transcription & summarization — every body-cam or interview video becomes searchable text + key-frame timelined."
   [LYC] "One-click redaction — faces, plates, minors' voices, and PII are masked with CJIS-compliant logs."
   [BDN] (Cheng) "Essentially, we make it so that the patrol is reviewing the reports rather than writing the reports
   from scratch"; "Code Four inserts extraneous, random or incorrect information into the reports. If an officer doesn't
   remove that information, they cannot submit a final draft." [CMP] "Every report fact links to the source clip,
   transcript, and timestamp". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (footage uploaded before
   the shift ends — tested; typed into the records system; time to read a draft) and Adoption friction (read and
   correct every draft — tested; delete the check words). Relative advantage's two benefits: [LYC] "cutting desk time
   by 60%" (shorter_time) and [CMP] "Code Four analyzes every frame of body camera footage, not just the audio"
   (less_worry); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $30 per officer a month; the cost is the officers' report time.
   [BI] "Cheng said Code Four works with 25 police departments and makes money via a subscription model, which starts
   at $30 per officer a month." [PR] "Code Four is significantly cheaper at $30 per officer per month. Sever estimated it
   would cost Heber City between $6,000 and $8,000 annually." → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $30 to $30 per officer
   (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, HOURS 40 to 60 of the incident reports per officer a month: author's arithmetic from [YCW] "up
   to a third of their shifts" and [LYC] "40% of a typical shift", on 8-to-10-hour shifts and about fifteen shifts a
   month (a third of 8 hours x 15 = 40; 40% of 10 hours x 15 = 60). The rate, $37 an hour, is [BLS] "The median annual
   wage for police and detectives was $77,310 in May 2025" ($37.17 an hour), the author's stand-in: no source gives an
   officer's hour. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [PR] (a Heber City sergeant, of a report drafted with an AI tool) "This report would have taken me an hour, and it
   took me eight minutes." [CMP] (a chief, vendor-curated) "Code Four helped one of my guys who was 3 weeks behind
   reports finish his reports" (the quote goes on; its last words are not reproduced here). [BDN] (a researcher) "There's
   a lot of error there because of background noise: being on the side of a highway, of trucks driving by".

## Status today

Widened, same core. [SITE] today sells four products (report writing, investigations over phone dumps and jail calls,
redaction, a mobile field-capture app) and claims "Live in 200+ departments"; [YCP] reads "Modernizing the police
workflow." Customer counts in the press: 25 departments ([BI] 2025-11-19), about 50 ([BDN] 2026-02-24). Price today:
no public price list ([SITE], read 2026-10-22); the latest dated figure is [BDN] "If the department decides to continue
using it, they will pay $50 per officer per month, or about $3,000 to $5,000 a year for the small department." (after a
free first year).

## Could not be sourced

- **A launch-era price.** Neither [LYC] nor the site's archived snapshot of 2025-07-01 carries one; the earliest dated
  price is [BI]'s $30 per officer a month, six months after launch. It is used as the founder's price because it is the
  nearest dated figure and the price the company named publicly first; a reader holding the entry to the launch era
  should treat the price as one step later than the rest.
- **An officer's hour.** No source gives one; [BLS]'s median for police and detectives stands in.
- **The hours per officer a month.** The founders give shares of a shift, not hours; the 40 to 60 is the author's
  arithmetic (item 7).
- **A buyer title for the cap.** Only Heber City's chief is on record ([PR]); that every chief has a cap, and that the
  council and city manager are the other roles, is the author's reading.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person officer accounts.** None exists; officer occasions are scripted from [PR], [BDN]
  and [CMP] (the last vendor-curated).
- The footage-upload condition (tested Compatibility), the three Purchase friction items but the trial, and every pick
  are the author's.

screens.why1: After how it fits the way officers work, asking what it does better is the obvious next step, and it is the reason a department would switch from hand-writing reports.
screens.why2: It is short and plain, and I can answer it at once in my own words: minutes instead of an hour, and nothing on the footage missed.
screens.why3: Desk time and what officers miss on the footage are exactly what I pitch to every chief, so I know the answer cold.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with one escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' is a fair way out for a founder who will not test advantage.
screens.why5: Keel kept 'minutes, not an hour' but dropped my second benefit, nothing on the footage left out, and its 'their last call would have gone better' credits the call rather than the report.
screens.instead: What does it do better than writing the report from the footage by hand? (e.g. the report done in minutes, not an hour; nothing on the footage left out)

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today's way, this is the obvious place to check the benefits Keel drew out of that answer.
screens.why2: Report, footage and "minutes, not an hour" are how my officers and I talk, and each row reads on first pass.
screens.why3: I know what my product saves officers and what they worry about missing, so I can judge these rows straight from my own pitch.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and fair, but my headline promise is missing: every fact tied to its clip, so the officer can stand behind the report and get off shift on time, not stuck at the desk.
screens.why5: The rows hold my desk-time and every-frame claims, but the test line says their 'last call would have gone better', and a cop hears 'call' as the scene itself, which my product does not touch; it should be the write-up of the call.
screens.instead: Rows: 'The report done in minutes, not an hour' / 'Nothing on the footage left out' / 'Every fact tied to its clip' / 'Off at end of shift, not stuck writing'; test: 'For most, writing up their last call would have gone better with it.'

screens.why1: After the screens on fit and advantage, asking what officers must do to start using it is the natural last piece of the solution step, and it is where the review-every-draft burden belongs.
screens.why2: "Setup, extra steps or learning" is plain to me as a founder selling to departments, and I can answer it in under 25 words without a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my product asks of an officer, because I designed the read-and-correct step and the inserted check words myself.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, and "Leave this out of the study" fits a free-text founder question with no wrong or missing choice.
screens.why5: The belief "Most would read and correct every draft before signing" keeps my tested burden word for word, and my check-word step stays in what I typed for the next screen to carry.

screens.why1: After I said what officers must do to start, Keel lists those steps back for me to check, which is exactly where adoption friction belongs.
screens.why2: Draft, signing, check words and body-cam footage are all words I and my officers use every day.
screens.why3: These are the steps I built into the product and that officers actually face on every report.
screens.why4: The two review steps are real, but uploading footage after each call overlaps with the Compatibility condition already tested and is something officers do anyway, not a new step.
screens.why5: The rows keep my mechanism as I typed it: officers review rather than write, must remove the inserted check words, and work from the footage.
screens.instead: What they'll have to do: Read and correct every draft before signing; Find and delete the check words in each draft; Learn to tag clips to the right call

screens.why1: Right after I checked what it takes to start, picking the one effort most likely to stop an officer is the obvious next step before the test is built.
screens.why2: Draft, signing and check words are my own words for the product and plain in the trade; the intro says nothing is reworded, so I know the officer sees my wording.
screens.why3: I know which effort my officers balk at: reading and correcting every draft is what Summit County's sergeant said ate the time savings, so I can pick it without guessing.
screens.why4: Reading drafts and deleting check words are real start-up efforts and distinct, but uploading footage after each call is the condition I already tested under Compatibility, so it overlaps a test I've done, and one I would have listed is missing: starting a report from the footage instead of a blank form.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most would read and correct every draft before signing' is word for word what I typed and puts the officer reviewing the report rather than writing it from scratch, which is my pitch; nothing about Code Four or the chief leaks into it.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? — Read and correct every draft before signing / Find and delete the check words in each draft / Start each report from the footage instead of a blank form

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the obvious place to decide whether to ask for a pilot, and a free pilot with no strings attached is exactly what I offer departments.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with yes/no and a one-line hint showing the email line is plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot sign-ups is my own call and I know the answer cold: yes, design-partner agencies are what I'm after.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a founder's own decision.
screens.why5: My pilot is run with a department and agreed by the chief, but the line goes to patrol officers who can't sign one up, and the screen doesn't let me say the pilot is the department's or ask for their chief.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Options: Yes, ask them to put me in touch with their department · Yes, ask for their own email · No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my questions just before the study goes out to officers is the obvious place for it, right after deciding on a pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question itself is plain, but the hint packs in video, typing, tapping, a one-time recording, 400 credits and text-message links, so I'd read it twice before I knew what I was actually choosing.
screens.why3: Which voice I want my officers to hear is my call to make, and I can make it by listening to two five-second samples.
screens.why4: Two named voices with samples and a default already picked is a complete, distinct choice, and with the price the same either way nothing is missing.
screens.why5: It names patrol officers as I typed them and changes nothing about my idea, and nothing about Code Four leaks into the choice of interviewer.
screens.instead: Who should ask patrol officers your questions? (Each officer gets a text link; the questions are spoken and also on screen. 400 credits either way.) — Daphne ▶ / Saskia ▶

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it is obvious that I'd pick how my officers answer before the link goes out.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but "She catches every spoken answer in a quiet room, and more than 9 in 10 where it is loud" makes me reread, and "Ready when Daphne is" only makes sense once I've read the first option.
screens.why3: I know how my officers work: they're on phones in cruisers or at the desk between calls, so I can judge whether they'd talk to a video or tap through.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and cover it (voice, text, either), and the readiness note on each is honest about what I can send now.
screens.why5: It keeps my officers as the ones answering and leaks nothing of Code Four's product to them; my pick, Read and tap, is offered as typed.

screens.why1: The study is built and the interview mode is set, so the last thing to settle is who gets the link — obvious at this point.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'the Contacts page' is Keel's own term I haven't seen yet, so I'd read that option twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly how I reach officers: by name through the design-partner agencies and the chiefs who introduce me.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct, but my real route is missing: a chief or sergeant passing the link to their patrol shift. The open-link option covers that only roughly, and a Google sign-in is an odd ask of officers on department devices.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed, and it keeps saying patrol officers.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated under the title with '4 answered' beside it, and each card adds '5 needed to call it', so I know nothing was called and why.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart, and the tally '3 too few · 7 people answered' sits against cards that each say '4 answered', so I need a second look to see that 3 counts cards and that only 4 of my 7 officers reached each question.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry the belief lines I checked, word for word, though Keel's solution statement above them is garbled ('the patrol officer the officer uploads ...', and the drafted report is said twice).
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: it doesn't say to get one more officer through each question, or why 3 of the 7 dropped out before them.
screens.why_b5: No claim goes past the answers: the low n is stated on every card and nothing is called held or not held.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits beside "5 needed to call it", but the header says "4 answered" while the count line says "5 answered · 4 counted", so I have to work out that it means 4 counted, with Luis's guess left out.
screens.why_b2: I can see what is counted (yes, yes with steps, no) over 4 people, but "your bar · 3 of 4 (no more than 1 in 3 say no)" mixes a count with a ratio, and the ghost cell takes a second look before I see that 4 for and 0 against already clears it.
screens.why_b3: The title is Compatibility and the belief line is the one I checked, word for word; the bar line drops "for most" but is still mine.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic; it doesn't tell me that one more counted officer would settle it, or that the officers to find are the ones whose cameras upload only at the dock.
screens.why_b5: It doesn't oversell 4 for and 0 against: the small n is said outright ("a lean, not a call"), every respondent is listed, and the uncounted guess is named.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 4 counted say the footage was up before the shift ended (Luis's guess not counted); one more counted officer settles it, ideally one whose camera uploads only when docked.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats the same 4 counted against 5 needed, so I know why there is no call.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts whether my last call would have gone better, over 4 counted officers with Luis shown as a ghost cell, and the marker sits at 3 of 4; the 'Better · 3 3 a lot · 0 a little' run is cramped but readable on first look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Relative advantage and the belief is my line word for word: the report done in minutes, not an hour.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't say that one more counted officer decides it, or that 3 of 4 already sit on the right side of my bar.
screens.why_b5: n is visible throughout, the low n is named ('a small group: a lean, not a call'), the hypothetical framing is flagged, and nothing calls 3 of 4 a held belief.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 officers say the report would have gone a lot better, which would clear your bar. One more counted answer decides it, so send the study to another patrol officer.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside its number, but the line under it says '4 answered' while the count line says '5 answered · 4 counted', so I have to work out that 5 answered and only 4 were counted against the 5 needed.
screens.why_b2: The four bars (2 yes, 2 yes-if-worth-it, 0 and 0 against) read at once, but the bar label mixes '3 of 4' with 'no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no', and the ghost fifth cell in the strip, so I had to look twice to see the four counted already clear the marker at 3.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would read and correct every draft before signing' are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't say that one more counted officer would settle it, or that half of the yeses hinge on the draft being clearly worth the read, which is the thing I'd have to prove in a pilot.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible, sets Luis aside as a guess, and calls four for and none against 'a lean, not a call' rather than a held belief.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 5 needed, all 4 for, but 2 only if the draft is clearly worth it. Get one more officer's answer, and show in the pilot that checking a draft beats writing it from scratch.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside "4 answered · 5 needed to call it", so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and "the report done in minutes, not an hour" are my belief word for word, as I checked it.
screens.why_b4: "5 needed to call it" implies I need one more officer, but the screen never says that, or what Kenji's answer means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: n is visible everywhere, the low count is named as too few to call, and the one dissent is shown as one person rather than a trend.
screens.why_b6: Kenji's quote tells me something I didn't write: simple reports already get done in the car between calls, and short staffing hurts more than paperwork, so my value is in the long reports, not every call.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 5 answered, so get one more officer; the one 'no difference' writes simple reports in the car and puts staffing first, so test the claim on long reports like DUIs, not every call.

screens.why1: A size screener as the very first screen makes sense; I'd expect them to check I'm the kind of department they want before asking about my reports.
screens.why2: Plain to me on one read, though I'd stop for half a second over whether they mean sworn officers or everyone including dispatch and records.
screens.why3: I know roughly how many sworn we have, so I can answer it straight; someone right near 10 or 200 might have to think about it.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it cleanly for a size cutoff, and no escape is the right call on a gate.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 10-to-200 range and says nothing about any product, and 'department' covers my sheriff's office or a transit or campus force too.
screens.why6: Short and easy to hear once, though 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is stiffer than just saying 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Does your department have between 10 and 200 sworn officers? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After checking my department size, asking whether I wrote a report from a call this week is the obvious next gate before asking about the last one.
screens.why2: We don't say 'call report', we say 'incident report', and 'by hand' reads to me as pen and paper, which I never do because I type mine into the RMS, so I'd stop and wonder whether to say no.
screens.why3: Writing reports after calls is most of what I do at the end of a shift, so I know straight away whether I did one this week.
screens.why4: Yes and No are right, but a gate shouldn't carry an escape at all, and here it carries two chips, one of them a sentence ('I can't recall one particular call') and one, 'I'd rather not say', that the rules say doesn't exist.
screens.why5: The point is writing the report myself from the call and its body-cam footage, but 'by hand' drifts toward handwriting, so an officer who types every report could truthfully answer No and get screened out.
screens.why6: Spoken as 'In the last 7 days, did you write up a call report by hand? Yes or no.' it is short, one question, and easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you write an incident report yourself after a call? Yes or no.

screens.why1: I've just said I wrote a report by hand this week, so being shown a tool that drafts reports from body-cam footage is the obvious next step for Part 2.
screens.why2: Narrative, records format, body-cam and redact are all my words, but 'check words you must catch' means nothing to me on first read, and calling Code Four 'a drafted narrative report' makes it sound like the report itself rather than the thing that writes it.
screens.why3: Turning a call's footage into the narrative is exactly the hour I lose after every arrest, so I can picture this against my own shift.
screens.why4: It is a card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The pitch comes through, but the opening line names the product as the report instead of saying what it does, and 'check words' reads like the builder's own term for a feature I am never told about.
screens.why6: It is far longer than three lines spoken, it piles four features into the 'how', and 'check words you must catch' trips the ear and would not register when heard once.
screens.instead: Imagine Code Four, a tool that drafts your incident report from the body-cam footage. After a call you upload the footage, and it writes the narrative in your department's report format, with each fact linked to its clip and a few planted mistakes you have to catch before you sign. The people building it believe you would review and sign instead of writing from scratch.

screens.why1: The card only says a drafted narrative report and never says it works from the body-cam, so being asked about uploading footage is plausible but comes a little out of nowhere.
screens.why2: Footage, uploaded and end of shift are how I talk about my body-cam every day, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I dock the camera at end of shift and it uploads on its own after that, so I often don't know if it finished before I clocked out and would be guessing.
screens.why4: 'Yes, with some steps' doesn't fit an upload that either happened or didn't; the real middle answer is 'only once I docked it at end of shift'.
screens.why5: The idea card names the product on purpose, and the question stays about my camera and my shift, with no product or role words leaking.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and three options plus 'you can't tell' are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Think of your last call. Was its body-cam footage up on the system before you wrote the report? Yes · Only after I docked the camera · No, it went up later · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea card and the footage question, asking whether Code Four would have helped on my last call is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Go better for you is plain, but a drafted narrative report as the whole description leaves me guessing what Code Four actually does with my footage, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I wrote up my last call myself, so I know whether a drafted narrative would have saved me the hour or the late clock-out.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and I can't tell fits when I don't trust what the draft would get right.
screens.why5: Calling the product itself a drafted narrative report drifts from the idea of a tool that drafts the report from body-cam footage, but nothing leaks beyond the card.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold, with the escape said last, said well.
screens.instead: Imagine Code Four, a tool that drafts your narrative report from the body-cam footage. Would it have made writing up your last call easier, or not? A lot easier, A little easier, No difference, Harder, or I can't tell.

screens.why1: After the idea card and asking whether it would have helped my last call, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually take on the review step it needs.
screens.why2: Reading and correcting a draft before I sign it is exactly how I already talk about reports with my sergeant, so I get it on the first hearing.
screens.why3: I sign every report I write and I know whether I'd go through an AI draft line by line, so I can answer it from my own shifts.
screens.why4: 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' blurs into plain 'Yes', and it reads oddly because my name goes on the report and I have to stand behind it anyway; the option that's missing is 'I'd skim it, not read every line', which is the honest answer for a lot of us at the end of a shift.
screens.why5: The card calls Code Four 'a drafted narrative report', but it's the thing that drafts the report, not the report itself, so the product drifts a little in how it's named.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is short and asks one thing, and the four options plus 'I can't tell' are easy to hold.
screens.instead: To use Code Four, you'd read and correct every draft before you sign it. Would you do that, or not? -- Yes, every line · I'd skim it and fix what jumps out · No · or I can't tell
